standard.title: Add and subtract two-digit numbers
standard.description: add and subtract one- and two-digit numbers, representing problems using number sentences, and solve using part-part-whole reasoning and a variety of calculation strategies
standard.prior_knowledge: Students add and subtract numbers within 20 using part-part-whole knowledge to 10 and a variety of calculation strategies (AC9M1N04). They have not yet extended these strategies to two-digit numbers or represented problems as number sentences.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students add and subtract one- and two-digit numbers by representing problems as number sentences and solving using part-part-whole reasoning and a range of strategies including bridging tens, near doubles, partitioning and number lines.

nodes.label: Number sentences for problems
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can represent an addition or subtraction situation as a number sentence and explain how each number in the sentence connects to the problem.
nodes.minimum_width: Write a number sentence for a given addition or subtraction situation; identify what each number in the sentence represents.
nodes.typical_width: Represent addition and subtraction problems using number sentences and bar models; explain the connection between each number and the situation; recognise that the same situation can be represented as both an addition and subtraction sentence.
wider: Use First Nations Australians' stories and dances to represent addition and subtraction relationships as number sentences; discuss how the two operations balance each other
Write number sentences for situations where one quantity is unknown (missing addend); explain how part-part-whole helps find the missing value
nodes.hinge_reason: Nodes 2 and 3 both require students to represent problems as number sentences before applying strategies. Students who cannot form a number sentence from a situation have no structure to reason from — strategy selection and application cannot occur.
success_criteria: Writes a correct number sentence for an addition or subtraction situation
Identifies what each number in the sentence represents in the context

nodes.label: Strategies for two-digit addition
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can add two-digit numbers using at least two strategies (e.g. bridging tens, partitioning, near doubles) and explain their reasoning.
nodes.minimum_width: Add two two-digit numbers using one mental strategy; explain the steps (e.g. partition, bridge to ten, combine).
nodes.typical_width: Apply strategies including near doubles, part-part-whole to 10, bridging tens and partitioning to mentally solve two-digit addition problems; use informal jottings to track steps; recognise that zero added leaves a number unchanged.
wider: Apply the associative property to rearrange addends for easier calculation: e.g. 7+8 = 7+(7+1) = (7+7)+1
Use a number line or hundreds chart to solve two-step addition problems; compare results with mental strategies and explain why they give the same answer

response_modes.reason: At this node students need to build a repertoire of strategies rather than rely on a single approach. Each strategy (bridging, partitioning, near doubles) suits different problem types — building range means students can select flexibly.

success_criteria: Correctly adds two two-digit numbers using a mental strategy
Explains the reasoning steps of the strategy used
Applies at least two different strategies to the same problem type

nodes.label: Strategies for two-digit subtraction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can subtract one- and two-digit numbers using part-part-whole reasoning and at least one mental strategy, and represent the problem as a number sentence.
nodes.minimum_width: Subtract a one- or two-digit number from a two-digit number using a mental strategy; represent as a number sentence.
nodes.typical_width: Apply strategies including counting back, bridging tens and partitioning to subtract one- and two-digit numbers; use informal jottings; connect subtraction to related addition facts (inverse relationship).
wider: Use a physical or mental number line to solve multi-step subtraction problems (e.g. gift card problem: $100 - $38 - $15)
Explore the inverse relationship by writing the related addition fact for a subtraction problem; discuss why knowing one helps you solve the other

response_modes.reason: Subtraction is more error-prone than addition at this stage because students may revert to counting back from the minuend rather than using efficient strategies. Working across multiple problem contexts — including those where the structure clearly suggests bridging or adding up — helps students see that the choice of strategy depends on the numbers involved.

success_criteria: Subtracts a one- or two-digit number from a two-digit number correctly
Represents the subtraction as a number sentence
